title: A Microfluidic Chip for the Versatile Chemical Analysis of Single Cells
protocol: Heat a 4 inch silicon wafer for 10 min at 180 °C.
Load the dehydrated wafer onto a spin-coater.
Spin the wafer at 100 rpm for 20 sec (open lid of spin-coater, dispense SU-8 during this step, close lid after dispensing).
Spin the wafer at 500 rpm for 10 sec to spread the resist over the whole wafer.
Spin the wafer at 1,750 rpm for 30 sec to define the height of the resist to 20 µm.
Remove resist from the edge of the wafer with acetone (use a swab).
Transfer the wafer to a hotplate at 95 °C and heat for 4 min.
Expose the resist through a photomask taped to sodalime glass in a mask aligner with UV light (150 mJ/cm², measured at 365 nm).
Heat the wafer again at 95 °C for 5 min on a hotplate.
Cool down the wafer to room temperature.
Immerse the wafer into a bath of SU-8 developer for 4 min.
Shake gently to remove unexposed SU-8.
Wash the wafer with clean-room grade isopropanol.
Blow dry the wafer with nitrogen.
Check under a microscope if the development was successful.
Bake the wafer in an oven for 2 hr at 180 °C to remove all residual solvent.
Check the height of the channels with a step profiler.
If necessary, develop the wafer again for a few minutes.
Dehydrate a silicon wafer for 10 min at 180 °C.
Spin-coat 1 ml HDMS onto this wafer at 7,500 rpm for 30 sec.
Expose the resist to UV-light (21 mJ/cm² at 365 nm) through a photomask and on a mask aligner.
Develop the resist in a bath of AZ 726 for 75 sec.
Rinse the developed wafer with DI-water.
Blow dry the wafer with nitrogen.
Remove residual solvent by heating the wafer at 115 °C for 50 sec.
Silanize the wafer under vacuum overnight.
Prepare a 10:1 mixture of PDMS and curing agent.
Mix both parts vigorously and degas the PDMS until the mixture is bubble free (~30 min).
Place the wafer with the control layer inside a Petri dish and tape it onto the bottom.
Pour ~50 g of PDMS on top and put the wafer for at least 2 hr in an oven at 80 °C to assure complete curing of the PDMS.
Repeat the same procedure for the microcontact printing wafer, using ~20 g PDMS.
Spin-coat PDMS on the wafer with the fluidic layer at a rotational speed of 2,000 rpm to form an approximately 40 µm high PDMS layer.
Cure the PDMS in an oven for at least 1 hr at 80 °C.
Remove the control layer from the wafer.
Cut the wafer into pieces with a razor blade.
Punch pressure connection holes using a 1 mm biopsy puncher.
Cover the channels with tape for storage.
Place the spin-coated wafer and top part in a plasma cleaner.
Align both parts under a microscope after plasma treatment.
Add spare PDMS around the placed top parts (optional).
Place the wafer in an oven at 80 °C for at least 1 hr.
Carefully remove the PDMS from the wafer using a scalpel.
Cut the microchips with a scalpel.
Punch access holes for fluidic connections with a 1.5 mm biopsy puncher.
Store the finished PDMS chip (optional: bond to a reservoir).
Clean a glass slide with soap, distilled water and ethanol.
Dry the cleaned glass slide using a nitrogen stream.
Clean the PDMS part with scotch tape.
Put the PDMS part and the cleaned glass slide into the plasma cleaner for 45 sec at 18 W.
Place the chip on a hot plate (100 °C) for 5 min to assure tight bonding.
Fill the fluidic channels with blocking solution using centrifugal force.
Incubate the blocking solution for at least 30 min at room temperature.
Wash the solution out of the fluid layer with PBS at a flow rate of 10 µl/min using a syringe pump.
Incubate PDMS stamps for microcontact printing with a bBSA/BSA solution (e.g., 1-100) for 30 min.
Clean the stamps thoroughly with distilled water and dry them under a stream of nitrogen.
Expose the glass slide and top part of the microfluidic chip to oxygen plasma for 45 sec at maximum power (18 W).
Remove the stamp after plasma treatment and align the printed surface underneath the microchambers of the device.
Place the chip on a hot plate at 50 °C for 30 min.
Introduce sterile-filtered BSA solution (4% (w/v) in PBS) into the chip using a centrifuge.
Incubate the chip with BSA solution for 1 hr.
Wash the BSA solution out of the fluid layer with PBS.
Store the chip directly or at 4 °C in a humid box for up to 2 weeks.
Introduce avidin (0.025% (w/v) in PBS) into the reservoir and flush at a flow rate of 5 µl/min for 30 min.
Flush PBS through the fluid channels for 10 min after withdrawing the avidin solution.
Rinse the reservoir thoroughly with PBS.
Add Protein G (0.0025% (w/v) in PBS) to the reservoir and flush for another 30 min.
Wash with PBS for an additional 10 min.
Next, add the antibody of interest (0.0001% (w/v) in PBS) and flush for 10 min.
Stop the flow after 10 min to allow binding for 15 min.
Finally, wash the chip with PBS for another 10 min.
Prepare cells according to the specific protocol.
For suspension cells, add cells directly to the chip.
For adhesive cell lines, use enzyme-free dissociation buffer to produce a cell suspension.
Filter the cells before introducing them to the chip to reduce the amount of cell clusters.
Load the cells onto the chip using a syringe pump and forward flow.
Use a flow rate of 5 µl/min for suspension cell lines.
Use higher flow rates of 10-20 µl/min for adhesive cells to reduce nonspecific attachment of the cells onto the channel walls.
When the traps are filled, close the chambers.
If many cells adhere nonspecifically to the surface, try to wash them away with cell dissociation buffer at a flow rate of 10-30 µl/min.
Withdraw lysis buffer through the chip.
For this example, use a hypoosmolar buffer with added Tween 20 (10 mM Tris-HCl, 10 mM KCl, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 1% (v/v) Tween 20).
For lysis, quickly open and close chambers (i.e., 500 msec for flow rates of 10-50 µl/min).
For the G6PDH assay, add 2 mM glucose-6-phosphate, 0.5 mM NADP, 0.5 U/ml diaphorase, and 0.3 mM resazurin to the lysis buffer.
Start monitoring the kinetic reaction immediately after lysis.
For ELISA, add the required detection reagent directly to the lysis buffer.
Add Tween 20 to reduce nonspecific adsorption.
Lysate cells according to step 5.4.
Incubate mixture for 10-15 minutes to allow binding.
Flush a permanent inhibitor of the used detection enzyme through the chip during incubation time.
Introduce the detection reagent (e.g., Amplex Red and hydrogen peroxide for HRP) to the chip after incubation.
Open chambers briefly to wash nonbound secondary antibody away and add detection reagent.
Start monitoring the kinetic reaction immediately.
Immobilize the antibody against the target of interest.
Prepare different concentrations of analyte in buffer or in cell lysate off-chip.
Apply a concentration of analyte to the chip and quickly exchange the volume inside the chambers (500 msec opening time).
Calculate the amount inside the chamber from the known concentration of antigen and the volume of 625 pl.
Introduce the detection moiety.
